strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem in LLM multi-agent systems (MAS): defending against adversarial propagation without relying on labeled attack data or prior knowledge of attack types.

The experimental evaluation is extensive, spanning multiple attack modalities (prompt injection, tool exploitation, memory poisoning), diverse communication topologies (chain, tree, star, random), and multiple LLM backbones (GPT-4o-mini, DeepSeek-V3, Qwen3-30B-A3B).

Consistently outperforms existing unsupervised graph anomaly detection baselines (DOMINANT, PREM, TAM) across varied settings and effectively approaches the performance of the supervised upper bound (G-Safeguard).
The paper is well-structured, clearly written, and accompanied by informative ablation studies examining the multi-level representations and scalability across agent counts.
weaknesses: The synthetic attack corruption is quite simplistic: it relies on injecting directionally uniform Gaussian noise into the SentenceBERT embedding space. The paper lacks deeper empirical or theoretical analysis demonstrating how well random isotropic noise in embedding space approximates subtle, semantically stealthy real-world attacks.

The anomaly scoring relies on average contextual similarity across all agents in the MAS. This assumes that normal agents exhibit high mutual semantic similarity, which holds in collaborative debate or consensus QA tasks, but may break down in heterogeneous role-playing multi-agent systems (e.g., ChatDev, MetaGPT) where agents possess specialized, complementary roles and naturally generate semantically divergent responses.

The remediation mechanism relies on a fixed budget of Top-K agents ($K=3$) being marked as malicious. In real-world deployments, the number of compromised agents is unknown; the paper does not adequately evaluate system degradation or false positive rates when no agents (0 attackers) or fewer than $K$ agents are compromised.

The baseline comparisons are exclusively restricted to graph anomaly detection algorithms; comparisons with simple agent-level or prompt-level defenses (e.g., LLM self-reflection/moderation or basic consensus filters) are omitted.

strengths: Practical and timely research problem: While most existing defenses for multi-agent systems (MAS) rely on supervised models trained on known attack patterns, this work tackles the realistic and challenging setting of defending against unknown attacks without labeled malicious data.

Well-motivated architecture: The combination of a multi-scale hierarchical agent encoder (ego, local neighborhood, and global context) with a corruption-guided contrastive learning detector provides an intuitive, lightweight, and effective way to model MAS interaction graphs without expensive end-to-end LLM fine-tuning.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The paper conducts experiments across diverse attack vectors (prompt injection, memory poisoning, tool exploitation), multiple communication topologies (chain, tree, star, random), and several LLM backbones (GPT-4o-mini, Qwen3-30B-A3B, DeepSeek-V3), clearly outperforming general unsupervised graph anomaly detection baselines.
weaknesses: Missing evaluation on benign/clean MAS execution: The paper does not thoroughly report the impact of BlindGuard on clean (unattacked) multi-agent workflows. Because the remediation scheme prunes the top-K highest anomaly nodes (fixed to K=3 in the setup), applying this defense when no attack is present—or when fewer than K agents are compromised—could inadvertently prune legitimate agents and degrade benign task accuracy.

Synthetic corruption vs. stealthy/adaptive attacks: The synthetic anomaly generator relies on adding scaled uniform Gaussian noise to SentenceBERT embeddings. In practice, sophisticated prompt injection or memory poisoning attacks produce synthetically coherent and task-aligned text that may lie close to the manifold of benign embeddings rather than behaving like isotropic noise. The robustness against subtle or adaptive adversaries is left largely unexplored.

Assumptions regarding agent homogeneity: Equation 7 defines the anomaly score based on average similarity to all other agents. In heterogeneous MAS where agents have starkly different roles and outputs (e.g., planner, code generator, verifier, database retriever), benign agents will naturally have low mutual embedding similarity. The paper does not clarify how role-based heterogeneity affects the anomaly scoring metric.

Absence of direct text-level guardrail baselines: Comparisons are restricted to general graph anomaly detection (GAD) methods (DOMINANT, PREM, TAM) and supervised G-Safeguard. Evaluating against standard LLM safety filters or text guardrails (e.g., Llama-Guard, input/output perplexity filtering) would better highlight the specific necessity of graph-level modeling.

strengths: Practical and timely problem formulation: Moving from supervised graph anomaly detection to an unsupervised framework is crucial for multi-agent system (MAS) security, as collecting labeled malicious agents for diverse and emerging attack types is often impractical in real-world deployments.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The paper evaluates BlindGuard across three major attack categories (direct prompt injection, tool exploitation, memory poisoning), four interaction topologies (chain, tree, star, random), and three distinct LLM backbones (GPT-4o-mini, Qwen3-30B-A3B, DeepSeek-V3).

Strong and consistent empirical gains over unsupervised baselines: BlindGuard markedly outperforms existing unsupervised graph anomaly detection methods (DOMINANT, PREM, TAM) across almost all benchmark settings, showing substantial improvements in detection AUC and significant reductions in Attack Success Rate (ASR).

Ablation and scalability analysis: The authors provide helpful ablations verifying the importance of both local neighborhood and global graph contexts, as well as scaling experiments on systems with up to 50 agents.
weaknesses: Simplicity of feature corruption vs. real-world stealthy attacks: The corruption mechanism relies on injecting magnitude-scaled directional Gaussian noise into SentenceBERT embeddings. It remains unclear whether this simple heuristic adequately captures sophisticated, semantic-preserving, or stealthy adversarial attacks that closely mimic benign agent behavior.

Potential vulnerability under heterogeneous agent roles or colluding attacks: The inference score relies on negative average similarity to all agents in the MAS. In systems with highly heterogeneous roles, debate dynamics, or multi-agent collusion, benign dissenting agents could be falsely flagged as anomalous, while colluding malicious agents might mutually lower their anomaly scores.

Fixed anomaly budget assumption: During inference and remediation, the method assumes a fixed budget of top-K agents ($K=3$) to prune. In practice, the number of compromised agents is unknown a priori, and sensitivity analysis regarding $K$ (e.g., false positives when $K > |V_{atk}|$) is not provided.
Presentation flaws: Figure 2 contains typos (e.g., 'Contrastive Leanrning'), and the abstract ends abruptly with an empty code repository placeholder ('The code is available at:').

strengths: Addresses an important and practical security challenge in LLM-based multi-agent systems: detecting and mitigating compromised agents without requiring prior knowledge or labeled examples of attack behaviors.

The proposed method, BlindGuard, is lightweight and conceptually well-motivated, integrating multi-scale graph context (individual, neighborhood, and global system) with an embedding-space noise corruption and contrastive learning framework.

Comprehensive empirical validation across diverse attack vectors (prompt injection, tool exploitation, memory poisoning), four distinct interaction topologies (chain, tree, star, random), and multiple LLM backbones (GPT-4o-mini, DeepSeek-V3, Qwen models).

Extensive analysis and stress-testing, including evaluation on clean data to verify zero utility degradation, scalability up to 50 agents, robustness under collusion and adaptive attacks, and thoughtful failure case analysis.
weaknesses: The noise generation function in Eq. (5) samples \(\epsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)\), which produces uniformly distributed random directions on the sphere; claiming this is 'semantics-aware directional corruption' (e.g., in Appendix H) is somewhat overstated since the directions are generated purely at random rather than guided by semantic gradients or task semantics.

The primary experimental results rely on a fixed detection budget (top-K with K=3) matched to the exact ground-truth count of compromised agents. Although threshold-based ablation is provided in Appendix E.3, dynamic detection without oracle knowledge of the number of attackers remains a challenge in open deployments.

The anomaly scoring metric in Eq. (7) averages cosine similarity across all system agents, which could produce false alarms in heterogeneous MAS where agents are explicitly designed to have diverse specialized roles, distinct styles, or contrasting perspectives (as partially reflected in Appendix I).

strengths: The paper addresses a highly practical and critical problem in LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS): defending against adversarial propagation without relying on labeled malicious samples or prior attack knowledge.

The proposed method, BlindGuard, is intuitively motivated and technically coherent, combining a multi-level hierarchical encoder (ego, neighborhood, and global context) with corruption-guided contrastive learning to establish an angular margin around normal behaviors.

Extensive empirical evaluation across multiple attack modalities (prompt injection, memory poisoning, tool exploitation), communication topologies (chain, tree, star, random), and LLM backbones (GPT-4o-mini, DeepSeek-V3, Qwen3 variants) demonstrates consistent improvements over existing unsupervised graph anomaly detection baselines.

The supplementary analysis is exceptionally thorough, covering cross-attack generalization, collusion attacks, adaptive attack scenarios, clean-data utility impact, computational complexity, and qualitative failure cases.
weaknesses: The noise injection mechanism in Eq. (5) is described as 'directional' and 'semantics-aware', but mathematically it samples standard isotropic Gaussian noise $\epsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$ scaled by magnitude. Characterizing purely random spherical perturbation in embedding space as semantics-aware is somewhat overstated.

The core defense relies fundamentally on the assumption that compromised agent responses exhibit significant semantic divergence from the group context. As honestly analyzed in the failure analysis (Appendix I), on-topic, stealthy attacks (e.g., subtly biased reasoning, manifold-preserving mimicry) can easily evade detection, while benign agents with diverse reasoning formats risk false isolation.

The main evaluation relies on a known budget of compromised agents ($K=3$) to identify anomalies. While Appendix E.3 investigates a fixed threshold, unsupervised threshold calibration in heterogeneous, dynamic multi-agent deployments remains non-trivial.

strengths: Practical and timely problem formulation: Shifting multi-agent system (MAS) defense from unrealistic supervised graph anomaly detection (which requires prior labeled malicious nodes) to an unsupervised setting trained strictly on benign interaction graphs.

Well-motivated hierarchical architecture: The hierarchical agent encoder cleanly unifies individual agent semantics, local neighborhood aggregation, and global system-level context, capturing both localized and coordinated multi-agent anomalies.

Extensive empirical evaluation: The paper conducts comprehensive experiments spanning four graph topologies (chain, tree, star, random), three distinct attack categories (prompt injection, tool exploitation, memory poisoning), and multiple LLM backbones (GPT-4o-mini, DeepSeek-V3, Qwen models).

Thorough supplementary studies: The submission provides valuable analyses on adaptive attacks, collusion attacks, clean accuracy preservation, scalability up to 50 agents, and an insightful failure mode analysis examining on-topic stealthy attacks versus benign reasoning style heterogeneity.
weaknesses: Heuristic nature of the anomaly synthesis: The training signal relies on injecting directionally isotropic Gaussian noise into SentenceBERT embeddings. While effective empirically, isotropic perturbation does not necessarily model real-world semantic adversarial manipulations, which often exhibit subtle, on-manifold semantic drifts rather than random vector shifts.

Strong assumption of homogeneity among benign agents: The unsupervised scoring function measures negative average cosine similarity to all other agents in the MAS. In realistic heterogeneous workflows (e.g., specialized multi-agent systems with distinct roles like planner, coder, tester, and critic), benign agents will inherently produce stylistically and semantically divergent outputs, which risks severe false-positive pruning.

Reliance on top-K budget in primary results: The main evaluation assumes a known attack budget (top K=3 compromised agents). While Appendix E.3 investigates thresholding, the practical challenge of dynamically and reliably setting anomaly thresholds across varying tasks without labeled calibration data remains underexplored.
